topics.title: planar IC process
topics.essence: A chip is made from the top down: grow oxide, coat it with photoresist, expose a pattern through a mask, etch windows and implant dopants through them. The designer draws lengths and widths; the process fixes depths, thicknesses and doping.
topics.check: Why can an IC designer choose a resistor's length and width but not its thickness?

topics.title: sheet resistance
topics.essence: A thin layer of fixed thickness has the same resistance across any square of it, whatever the square's size: R_□, in ohms per square. A resistor is R_□ times its number of squares, L/W.
topics.check: A 10 μm by 10 μm square of a layer measures 200 Ω edge to edge. What does a 1 μm square measure, and a strip 50 μm long and 5 μm wide?

topics.title: IC capacitor
topics.essence: Two conducting layers with thin oxide between them form a parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε_ox·A/t_ox. The process fixes the oxide thickness, so the capacitance per area is fixed and the designer chooses only the area.
topics.check: You halve the oxide thickness and halve the plate area. What happens to the capacitance, and to the voltage it can safely hold?

topics.title: small-signal capacitance
topics.essence: When stored charge is not proportional to voltage, capacitance is the slope dQ/dV at the bias point. A small wiggle in voltage moves the charge by C times the wiggle, and C changes when the bias changes.
topics.check: A junction's charge grows as the square root of its reverse voltage. Does its small-signal capacitance rise or fall as the reverse bias grows, and why?

topics.title: transconductance
topics.essence: Transconductance g_m is how much output current changes per volt at the input: the slope at the bias point. A MOSFET gives g_m = 2I_D/V_OV and a BJT g_m = I_C/(kT/q), so at the same current the BJT gives more.
topics.check: A MOSFET with V_OV = 0.2 V and a BJT each carry 1 mA. Which has the larger g_m, and by about how much?

links.why: Implanting dopants through windows in the oxide is how doped regions get their shapes.
Lump the resistivity and the fixed thickness into one number, R_□ = ρ/t.
The process fixes the layer's thickness and doping, which is why only L/W is left to the designer.
The charge on one plate sets a uniform field across the oxide, and the voltage is that field times the thickness.
Grown oxide is the dielectric, and its thickness is set by the process.
For a plate capacitor the slope dQ/dV and the ratio Q/V agree; in a semiconductor they do not.
Differentiate the square law: g_m = μC_ox(W/L)V_OV = 2I_D/V_OV.
Differentiate I_C = I_S·e^(qV_BE/kT): the slope is I_C/(kT/q) at any current.
